newsitem.title: USA: Bell Atlantic, NYNEX not worried by FCC review.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic, NYNEX not worried by FCC review.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp. and NYNEX Corp. do not expect federal regulators to attach onerous conditions to their proposed $23 billion merger, according to sources at both Baby Bells.
At worst, the Federal Communications Commission may require the companies to report progress in opening their markets to local competition, the sources said.

The sources, responding to a Wall Street Journal report that the FCC was holding up approval of the merger, said they saw nothing surprising in the latest round of questions coming from FCC staff reviewing the deal.
"None of this is terribly new," one source said. "We're not talking about them requiring a major business restructuring or spin-offs."

Another source said, "I think we're looking mostly at reporting requirements, although I can't say whether any one thing has been proposed. We've been having talks like this now for months, and certainly more so since (the FCC) requested the additional information."

An FCC source said that in the agency's view, it was not accurate to characterise the FCC review of the merger as a delay. The FCC is following the same steps it would take with any other merger of this size, the source said.

In early June the FCC sent NYNEX and Bell Atlantic a seven-page list of additional documents to be submitted as part of the final review. Sources at the companies and the FCC said the agency was seeking assurances that the companies were taking significant steps to open their Northeast and Mid-Atlantic markets to new local phone competitors in compliance with the Telecommunications Act of 1996.

FCC approval is the final regulatory hurdle the two companies must clear in order to complete the merger, announced in April 1996. The Justice Department approved the deal in April, attaching no conditions.
Neither company expected the merger proposal to win FCC approval before agency Chairman Reed Hundt returned to Washington this week from an overseas trip, the sources said.
Analysts agreed that the FCC's apparent insistence on a thorough review was not surprising.

"Reed Hundt emphatically supports the notion of open competition in the local phone markets as spelled out in the Telecommunications Act, and what's happening is consistent with that," said Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Frank Governali.

"The FCC is really trying to use the public interest writ made available in the act to the fullest to ensure some protection for consumers in the markets covered by these two," said Prudential Securities analyst Susan Lynner. "It's not surprising at all that the FCC is taking a long look at this."
Lynner said the scrutiny is even less surprising given Hundt's stance that the FCC "will not be the Justice Department's handmaiden."
